e.etymology: From Arabic abd, servant, and Allah, God. Abd Allah was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's father; Abdallah is one of several English spellings of the same name as Abdullah.
A C spelling of Serenity, the English word for calm, from Latin serenus, clear and tranquil. Serenity became a popular girls' name in the late 1990s.
An old Arabic name usually traced to marw, flint or quartz, a hard stone used to strike fire. It is best known from Marwan I, the Umayyad caliph whose line ruled from Damascus.
A spelling of Khalil, Arabic for an intimate friend. Khalil Allah, friend of God, is the traditional Islamic title of Abraham.
A transliteration of Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God?, the name of the archangel Michael. The kh keeps the sound of the Hebrew and Greek originals; Arab Christians are among those who use this form.
A respelling of Mason with the fashionable Mae. Mason is an English occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French maçon.
A surname in both England and Italy, from Middle English pais and Italian pace, peace, both from Latin pax. It is also the ordinary English word for speed or a step.

assoc.t: pace, the word for speed or a single step

e.meaning: dahlia flower; in Hebrew, hanging branch
e.etymology: A spelling of Dalia, which is Spanish for the dahlia flower (named for Swedish botanist Anders Dahl), a Hebrew name meaning hanging branch, and a girls' name in Arabic as well.
A Latin American spelling of Scarlett, an English surname for a dealer in scarlet, a fine cloth, from Old French escarlate. Scarlett O'Hara of Gone with the Wind made it a first name.

assoc.t: Scarlett O'Hara of Gone with the Wind (same sound)

e.etymology: A respelling of Winston, an English surname from the Old English personal name Wynnstan, wynn, joy, plus stan, stone, or from villages named Winston. The y echoes the original wynn.

assoc.t: Winston Churchill, wartime prime minister (same sound)

e.etymology: Two sources: a Finnish name taken from Lake Inari in Lapland, and Inari, the Shinto deity of rice, foxes and prosperity honored at Kyoto's Fushimi Inari shrine.

assoc.t: Inari, the Shinto deity of rice and foxes
inari sushi, rice in a sweet fried tofu pouch

e.etymology: The everyday Hebrew and Yiddish pet form of Yosef (Joseph), from the Hebrew for he will add. In the US it is used mostly in Orthodox Jewish families.
A K spelling of Coleson or Colson, an English surname meaning son of Cole, where Cole is an old short form of Nicholas or the Old English byname Cola, coal-dark.
The Scandinavian spelling of Christine, from Latin Christina, a follower of Christ, from Greek khristos, anointed. It was widely used in the US in the 1960s and 70s.
A 20th-century elaboration of Rachel in the French style, in step with Michelle and Rochelle. Rachel is Hebrew for ewe and the name of Jacob's beloved wife in Genesis.
From the English word brook, a small stream, by way of the surname for someone who lived beside one, from Old English broc. The spelling Brooke is more common for girls.

assoc.t: brook, the word for a small stream

e.etymology: A name used mostly in Mexico and among Latino families in the US since the 1970s. Its source is uncertain; it is often linked to Hebrew yadid, friend or beloved.
A nickname for Charles that grew out of Chas., the old written abbreviation of the name. Charles comes from Germanic karl, free man.
namesakes: Chaz Bono (writer and actor, child of Sonny and Cher)

e.etymology: An African American coinage of the later 20th century that joins the prefix Ty-, as in Tyrone and Tyrell, to Shawn, the phonetic spelling of Irish Seán (John).

A short form of Giovanna in Italy and of Ivanna in Slavic languages, both feminine forms of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. US use peaked in the 1980s with Wheel of Fortune's Vanna White.

assoc.t: Vanna White, letter-turner on Wheel of Fortune

e.etymology: A modern blend of Emma (from Germanic ermen, whole) and the -lyn ending, close in sound to the older Emmeline.

In the US mainly a K spelling of Cannon, a surname (from a church canon, or Irish Ó Canáin) and the word for the big gun. Kanon is separately a Japanese girls' name, often written with characters for flower and sound.

assoc.t: sounds like cannon, the large artillery gun

e.etymology: The Spanish Bible's form of Keziah, the second of Job's daughters, from Hebrew qetsiah, cassia, a fragrant bark like cinnamon.

e.meaning: dahlia flower; in Hebrew, hanging branch
e.etymology: A spelling of Dalia with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah. Dalia is Spanish for the dahlia flower, a Hebrew name meaning hanging branch, and a girls' name in Arabic as well.
A pet form of the Yiddish name Frayda (Freyde), from freyd, joy, a cousin of German Freude. In the US it is used almost entirely in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish families.

assoc.t: fraidy-cat, a childhood taunt for a scared person

e.note: Matches fraidy, as in fraidy-cat, the childhood taunt for someone easily scared.

e.etymology: The English word for the hard iron alloy, from Old English style. As a surname, also spelled Steele, it was a nickname for someone as tough and reliable as steel.

assoc.t: Steel, DC Comics hero in powered armor

e.etymology: A respelling of Eleanor that writes in the nickname Elle. Eleanor comes from Old French Aliénor, the Occitan name of Eleanor of Aquitaine, whose origin is uncertain.

A spelling of Tallulah, from Tallulah Falls and the Tallulah River in Georgia, a Cherokee place name of uncertain meaning. Actress Tallulah Bankhead made it famous. The Irish name Talulla is unrelated.
A modern Indian name built on Sanskrit shri, radiance, prosperity and good fortune, a word also used as a name of the goddess Lakshmi and as a title of respect.

A modern American spelling of Ellory, a twist on the surname Ellery with the sound of Mallory and the nickname Ellie built in. Ellery is a medieval English form of Hilary, from Latin hilaris, cheerful.
Elaia is a Basque girls' name from elai, the swallow, and also the ancient Greek word for the olive tree.
The French form of Monica, the name of Saint Augustine's North African mother. Its root is unknown, probably Punic or Berber; a later tradition tied it to Latin monere, to advise.
namesakes: Mo'Nique (comedian and Oscar winner for Precious)
